source.title: Harmless Interpolation of Noisy Data in Regression
source.authors: Vidya K. Muthukumar; Kailas Vodrahalli; Vignesh Subramanian; Anant Sahai

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices; no apparent truncation or garbling that prevents extraction.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives its own theoretical and empirical results on noisy interpolation in overparameterized linear regression and qualifies when interpolation helps or harms test MSE. It does not test the neural-network settings named in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates linear regression with Gaussian, Fourier, and polynomial features, not the neural-network or training settings in V1–V8. Its linear-regression findings are recorded under fits_no_version. Cited results about deep networks and other studies are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The study analyzes interpolation and excess prediction MSE in linear regression, rather than the neural networks and interventions named in V1–V8. Its feature-count experiments do not test neural-network width in V2. Section 6.1 explicitly leaves the implications for deep neural networks unresolved.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate but omits a central qualification: the authors conclude that denoising is preferable to interpolation in the correctly specified linear model, although extreme overparameterization can make interpolation's additional cost small. Minimum-norm methods can dissipate signal, sparse methods can fit noise poorly, and suitable hybrid methods achieve order-optimal rates under the stated assumptions. Extension to deep neural networks remains unresolved.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes interpolating linear regression procedures and feature families, not neural-network training recipes or the interventions in V1–V8.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported behavior depends on feature family and weighting, data sampling regularity, signal sparsity or misspecification, and the degree of overparameterization.

fits_no_version.finding: For Gaussian features, the ideal interpolator has excess test MSE of order σ²n/d in the strongly overparameterized regime.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Extreme overparameterization can make the unavoidable prediction cost of noisy interpolation vanish in linear regression.

fits_no_version.finding: Minimum-norm interpolation approaches null risk for the sparse isotropic Gaussian example but exhibits double descent for the constant-signal, nonzero-mean Gaussian example.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The generalization benefit of additional linear-regression features depends on feature structure and alignment with the signal.

fits_no_version.finding: Sparse interpolators preserve signal better in the reported example but dissipate pure noise slowly; hybrid signal estimation followed by residual interpolation closely tracks ideal MSE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Separating sparse signal estimation from noise interpolation can improve prediction in noisy overparameterized linear regression.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE Journal on Selected Areas in Information Theory
record.problems: Several numerical comparisons are presented in figures without exact values in the text. Empirical examples use small sample sizes in some sections; theoretical claims are restricted to stated feature-distribution assumptions. The ideal interpolator is not practically implementable because it requires the true signal.
record.rows_left_out: No additional study results matching V1–V8 were identified. Figure-only numerical points were not reconstructed as separate rows.

untested.parts: Matched neural-network training on natural versus random labels, including training fit and held-out accuracy.
Test error after widening ReLU networks beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Own benchmark comparisons of adaptive optimizers versus SGD under limited or broader tuning.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects on held-out classification error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and rankings against alternative measures.
Retraining after removing memorized examples versus equal-sized random removals.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels apply. The study's own results concern a different system and outcome; cited neural-network findings are background evidence.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare neural networks trained on natural labels with the same networks trained on random labels.
Does not test one-hidden-layer ReLU networks on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10.
Does not compare convolutional and fully connected image classifiers.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers with SGD or momentum SGD.
Does not compare batch sizes or training recipes for image classifiers or language models.
Does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness or compare it with generalization gaps.
Does not identify or remove memorized training examples.

rows.subject: ideal interpolator
rows.operation_detail: Derives bounds on the minimum possible test MSE among interpolating solutions as feature count increases.
rows.measure: Test MSE minus irreducible noise error
rows.value: The paper states that the ideal test MSE is at most O(σ²n/d) for Gaussian features and tends to 0 as d grows relative to n.
rows.uncertainty: High-probability bounds are stated in Corollaries 1 and 2; see source for probabilities and constants.
rows.note: The result concerns the ideal interpolator, which the paper says requires knowledge of the true signal and is a fundamental limit rather than a practical procedure.
rows.check: Valid theoretical linear-regression result, but it measures no claim version. Corollary 1 supplies lower bounds; Corollary 2 supplies the matching upper bounds under stronger assumptions. The ideal interpolator requires the true signal.

source_check.locator_found: Corollary 1, Eq. (5); Corollary 2, Eq. (6); Section 3.2, pp. 8–10.

rows.subject: minimum-ℓ2-norm interpolator
rows.operation_detail: Evaluates test MSE as the number of Gaussian features increases for a 500-sparse signal.
rows.baseline: Zero-fit test error is the null-risk reference described in text.
rows.value: The paper states that test MSE converges to the same level as using α = 0 and describes this example as performing extremely poorly.
rows.note: The text describes the qualitative trend; the figure contains the plotted values.
rows.check: Linear-regression null-risk convergence does not establish a reversed effect for any version. The measure is excess test MSE, subtracting irreducible noise, as defined in Section 2.

rows.subject: minimum-ℓ2-norm interpolator
rows.operation_detail: Evaluates test MSE as the number of Gaussian features increases for a misspecified constant-signal example.

conditions.value: constant 1, not exactly representable by a finite feature set

rows.value: The paper states that test MSE decreases with increased overparameterization and that the example shows double-descent behavior.
rows.note: The paper attributes part of the behavior to improved approximability from adding features, while stating this is not the main reason.
rows.check: Increasing Gaussian feature count in minimum-norm linear regression does not measure widening a trained ReLU network. The reported double descent concerns excess test MSE.

rows.subject: OMP run to completion and basis pursuit (BP)
rows.operation_detail: Evaluates test MSE against feature count for sparse linear regression with noisy observations.
rows.baseline: Ideal interpolator is plotted as a reference.
rows.value: The paper states OMP and BP are significantly better than the minimum-ℓ2-norm interpolator and appear only an extra noise multiple above the ideal interpolator.
rows.note: The stated qualitative comparison covers the three noise variances shown in Figure 7; separate plotted values are not described in the text.
rows.check: This comparison of linear-regression estimators measures no version. Split OMP and BP and the three noise conditions if retaining these auxiliary results. The measure subtracts irreducible noise.
